all_scored.title: FM4SAR-Bench 1.0: Towards A Fair Benchmark for Evaluating Foundation Models for SAR Image Interpretation
all_scored.summary: Foundation models have advanced SAR image interpretation but created a heterogeneous, fragmented model ecosystem. Existing models differ substantially in their input, training data, objectives, architectures, and release policy, yet the field lacks a unified taxonomy and comparative framework. Current evaluations rely primarily on task-specific benchmarks, which are ill-suited to fair comparison among models with fundamentally different input-output formats and task paradigms, and often overlook data transparency, reproducibility, interpretability, and deployment readiness. Limited SAR data accessibility also means high reported performance does not guarantee access to training data, code, or weights, limiting reproduction, benchmarking, and deployment. To address these issues, we propose a systematic taxonomy and hierarchical evaluation framework for SAR-related foundation models: five rating levels, six dimensions, and fine-grained criteria, with separate protocols for VFMs and VLMs. Beyond overall ratings, it yields interpretable multidimensional capability profiles and supports user-defined weighting, so rankings follow user priorities. Utilizing a fixed auxiliary multimodal large language model in combination with human review, we conduct a systematic meta-analysis and multidimensional assessment of 76 VFMs and 40 VLMs. In terms of SAR benchmark task performance under our framework, SAR-native VLMs do not significantly outperform remote sensing VLMs pretrained on mixed multimodal corpora in which SAR is one of several modalities. This lack of clear advantage is largely due to data availability: large-scale, high-quality, public annotated SAR data remain scarce, restricting both model and training-data scale for SAR-native models. The framework provides a structured basis for requirement-aware model selection and remains extensible as new models emerge.

all_scored.title: EgoSurgHands: An Egocentric 3D Hand Pose Dataset & Benchmark for Open Surgery Training
all_scored.summary: Surgical skill assessment, AR guidance, and robot learning from demonstration all benefit from 3D tracking of the surgeon's hands, yet no surgical dataset offers real egocentric articulated 3D hand pose. We introduce EgoSurgHands, a benchmark for real-captured egocentric hand pose estimation in open surgery training on synthetic pads. Captured with multi-sensor glasses, it contains 41,909 training hand-instance rows across 55 procedure recordings and 9,476 human-validated evaluation rows across 13 held-out recordings, spanning 13 tasks, 3 glove colors, and 4 trainees from first-year medical student to third-year resident. Each frame carries a multi-sensor stack: intrinsics, hand landmarks with per-hand confidence, timestamps, and eye gaze, plus SLAM extrinsics where SLAM succeeded. Evaluation labels combine sensor-fused pseudo-ground truth, human cross-review of every frame, surgeon adjudication of flagged cases, and an independent multi-view triangulated reference. Alongside the within-corpus, procedure-disjoint split, a leave-one-wearer-out protocol tested unseen trainees. Across eight methods evaluated zero-shot, from MANO-based reconstructors to the two-hand IntagHand and the keypoint-only MediaPipe Hands, egocentric pretraining was associated with stronger transfer on every held-out wearer. WildHands and JointTransformer had 18\% and 40\% lower PA-MPJPE, respectively, than the non-egocentric HaMeR. JointTransformer was the best performing model with an error of 14.95 mm. A substantial surgical domain gap remains, and the widely deployed MediaPipe Hands detected a hand in only 24.1\% of evaluation rows. As a baseline, a 58K-parameter residual corrector (JRN) on frozen backbones reached 10.96-14.85 mm PA-MPJPE on held-out wearers for the two ego-pretrained backbones. We release the dataset and benchmark code at https://egosurghands.github.io

all_scored.title: Epistemic Guard: Out-of-Process MCP Receipt Proxying, Post-Turn Prose Supervision, and Provenance-Gated Memory for Tool-Using Autonomous Agents
all_scored.summary: Language-model agents using the Model Context Protocol (MCP) face three runtime verification gaps: (i) action fabrication, where post-tool prose narrates side effects that failed, timed out, or never ran; (ii) provenance collapse, where unverified model prose or web text enters durable memory alongside executed tool outputs; and (iii) syndicated echo amplification, where mirrored web pages satisfy multi-source corroboration from one origin. Existing MCP firewalls inspect wire calls before execution, while LLM-judge guardrails require multi-gigabyte VRAM without binding prose to receipts. We present epistemic-guard (v0.5.2), an open-source Python library and out-of-process stdio MCP receipt proxy (15 modules, 0 MiB GPU VRAM). epistemic-guard isolates Ed25519 signing keys out of process, writes RFC 6962 Merkle logs with AER-1 receipt translation, checks post-turn prose on CPU with SHA-256-verified OpenVINO INT8 encoders (4 models, 279.48 MB total; 82.67 MB on the supervision path), gates SQLite writes across 7 provenance domains, and collapses verbatim and lightly edited wire-syndicated RAG mirrors. On conformance suites, epistemic-guard rejects 100.0% of tampered receipts (200 Merkle leaves), passes 58/58 official AER-1 ingestion vectors and 50/50 reference-verified AER-1 exports, verifies 100.0% of 40 fault-injected wire calls and 100 concurrent appends with 0 key leaks, and blocks 100.0% of 100 unauthorized memory writes. Across $N=250$ frozen-benchmark traces, epistemic-guard reaches 93.2% accuracy at 17.9 ms warm median CPU latency (8.62 ms single-clause; 921.8 ms cold-start load), beating 12B-14B GPU judges by 6.4-6.8 points ($p=0.0259$, $p=0.0095$) at 4.26-4.5$\times$ lower latency; on $N=60$ live mcp-proxy traces, it catches 96.15% of hazards at 76.67% accuracy (38.24% FPR; $+18.34$ points over Stage-1-only, $p=0.001$) in 9.16 ms p50.

all_scored.title: Mind World Models: Joint Learning of Motor EEG Representations and Action-Conditioned World Dynamics
all_scored.summary: Motor decoding from electroencephalography (EEG) supports non-invasive brain-computer interfaces, yet existing methods either rely on costly cue-based trials and coarse categorical labels or use pretraining objectives that do not directly capture how movement unfolds, limiting their ability to learn transferable motor representations. To this end, we propose the Mind World Model (MWM), a framework that learns motor EEG representations from scalable naturalistic EEG and egocentric video without action annotations. MWM treats EEG observed up to the current frame as the latent action of a world model: a mind model encodes the EEG, and a world model uses it to predict the representation of a future frame, yielding a movement-grounded pretraining objective. We further introduce the Lateralization-Aware Transformer (LAT), which uses frame averaging to separate shared bilateral from side-specific lateral features, encoding hemispheric correspondence to reduce the burden of learning left-right relationships from data. MWM pretraining produces two models: a mind model for downstream motor decoding and a world model that can be adapted to prediction conditioned on real actions, opening a scalable and flexible path to collect egocentric data for embodied AI. Across 9 classification and 7 regression tasks, the mind model improves task-averaged balanced accuracy by 5.9% and Pearson correlation by 16.2% relative to the strongest baseline in each task family. Compared with an inverse-dynamics latent-action baseline, the world model achieves lower prediction error and benefits 3.3 times more from matched real actions within recordings and 4.7 times more on held-out subjects.

all_scored.title: Keep the Process, Change the Supplier: Runtime Governance for Tool-Using AI Agents
all_scored.summary: Tool-using AI agents propose actions whose authorization and external effects cannot be inferred from generated text alone. We study an execution boundary that separates agent proposals from business-controlled authority, context disclosure, and supplier selection. The Open Process Control Plane (OPCP) mediates capability calls and records uncertain outcomes when a supplier may have acted without returning an acceptable reply. We evaluate this runtime with scripted requests and synthetic suppliers: 2,400 fault episodes across four policies, 60 process-termination/restart episodes, 19,000 timed calls across 19 configurations, five targeted mutations over 43 fixtures, and 160 substitution records. No language model or autonomous agent is evaluated. OPCP and a conservative composition agree on all measured fault outcomes. Both recover after definite refusal without cross-supplier duplication; retry-all duplicates effects in every tested lost-reply-after-commit case. Persistent runtime state prevents cross-supplier replay in the restart experiments, while same-supplier duplicate prevention also requires supplier idempotency. At 128 suppliers, best-score routing has a median latency of 1.411 ms versus 0.261 ms for pinned routing. All five selected mutations are detected, and record enumeration exposes acceptance of an empty regression set. These results characterize an execution mechanism relevant to agent governance, including its costs and assumption boundaries. They do not establish improved agent task success, prompt-injection resistance, or real-vendor model portability.

all_scored.title: CodeReviewBench: An Automated Benchmark for Evaluating the Software Factory
all_scored.summary: As AI agents ship more code with minimal human oversight, code review becomes the critical quality-control checkpoint -- but one without a reliable, objective verifier: review quality is nuanced and ultimately a judgment call by the PR author. Existing benchmarks are structurally misaligned with this: annotators are third-party reviewers, like the bots they evaluate, not the PR authors who actually decide what to fix. They also rely on small, static issue sets that require full re-evaluation as tools update, limiting how frequently progress can be tracked. We introduce CodeReviewBench, built on a fundamentally different signal: revealed developer preferences -- if a developer acts on a bot's suggestion, we treat it as useful; if they ignore it, we do not. This signal is mined daily from the public GitHub event stream, yielding 500K+ judged PRs across 18 tools, and refreshes continuously as tools evolve. We validate the developer preference against an independent offline benchmark: the two agree on precision rankings and independently detect the same product updates within days of vendor releases. Together, these form the benchmark.

all_scored.title: How Long Will My Language Model Run? A Benchmark for Pre-Execution Runtime Prediction
all_scored.summary: Researchers submitting deep learning jobs to shared GPU clusters need runtime estimates to request time limits, choose hardware, and budget compute. Large language models (LLMs) offer a tempting shortcut: describe the job and ask. We introduce PreRun, a benchmark for predicting deep learning training and inference runtime from information available before execution. PreRun contains 801 training and 1,884 inference records of language and vision models collected on a GPU cluster, paired with workload configurations and explicitly defined timing targets. It also includes 64 text-generation configurations measured under standardized conditions, each in three separate program launches. We compare three LLMs (Qwen3.5-9B, GPT-OSS-120B, and Claude Opus 5.5) with regression baselines and evaluate analytical estimates on a supported forward-pass subset. On 16 held-out generation configurations, the open-weight LLMs underestimate latency by 90-99% on average without examples. Claude's zero-shot mean absolute error is 4.5 times that of a Random Forest fit on 32 configurations. Five labeled examples substantially reduce Claude's generation error, but their benefit varies across timing targets. We will open-source our data and evaluation pipeline upon acceptance.

all_scored.title: Graph-XGB: A Hybrid GNN Framework for Outdoor-to-Indoor 5G Signal Reconstruction via Aerial-Only UAV RF Sensing
all_scored.summary: Delivering robust In-Building Coverage (IBC) is critically impeded by severe Outdoor-to-Indoor (O2I) attenuation, a constraint that intensifies as deployments move from 5G mid-band towards mmWave and prospective 6G sub-THz carriers, where losses of 60-80 dB have been reported across modern building envelopes. While Unmanned Aerial Vehicles (UAVs) offer scalable exterior RF sensing platforms, a fundamental inversion problem persists: interior 3D signal states cannot be directly sampled from constrained exterior flight paths. This paper proposes Graph-XGB, a hybrid inference framework that decouples spatial topology reasoning from non-linear signal regression to resolve this challenge. A modified SpiderGNN encoder, operating on a topology-aware graph constructed with a physically grounded Floor-Aware 3D Distance metric and Bridge Edge Guarantees, propagates UAV boundary measurements into 128-dimensional indoor embeddings. Principal Component Analysis (PCA) compresses these into a 10-dimensional manifold retaining 96.6% of embedding variance, fused with raw spatial features and decoded by independent, physics-tailored XGBoost regressors. This decoupling mitigates the optimization conflict between smoothly decaying path-loss signals and volatile interference-dependent metrics. Evaluated on a real-world 5G NR dataset of 613 verified nodes spanning the 10 floors of a single building, Graph-XGB attains the strongest accuracy among the architectures compared, with $R^2$ of 0.759 (RSSI) and 0.770 (RSRP), improvements of 35.5% and 64.9% over the SimpleGNN baseline, using no interior RF measurement as a model input; indoor observations enter only as training supervision, with evaluation on held-out internal nodes. Interference-dependent targets (RSRQ, SNR and CQI) remain bounded well below the path-loss metrics, delimiting the reach of purely spatial inference.

all_scored.title: Latent Space Planning with Sequential Monte Carlo
all_scored.summary: Planning with learned world models amounts to finding action sequences whose predicted rollouts reach a goal. Sampling-based planners often struggle at longer horizons, while gradient-based methods can become trapped in local minima. Meanwhile, model predictive path integral control (MPPI), a complementary approach, alternates between estimating an expectation under a cost-weighted distribution from samples and updating the plan from this estimate. Its samples, however, are drawn afresh at every iteration from a Gaussian proposal and reach the target distribution only through importance weights. Moreover, a target distribution favoring goal-reaching trajectories can be difficult to define directly, motivating a sequence of intermediate distributions. Sequential Monte Carlo (SMC) provides a natural mechanism for evolving such a sequence through importance weighting and resampling. Motivated by this, we formulate latent-space planning as optimization guided by SMC, which moves a population of action sequences while a gradient-based optimizer updates the plan. Inspired by classical planning, we further introduce a PDE-derived cost-to-go that guides the evolution of the sample distribution using the structure of the latent state space. On navigation and manipulation tasks with visual and proprioceptive world models, our formulation outperforms gradient-based planners by $29$ and $50$, sampling-based planners by $35$ and MPPI by $7$ percentage points in average success rate, while succeeding in fewer iterations than gradient-based planners and within 4\% of MPPI.

all_scored.title: Adding One More Agent: How AI Team Size and Formation Shape Productivity and Diversity in Human-AI Brainstorming Teams
all_scored.summary: Generative AI has improved individual productivity, but whether adding a plurality of AI partners helps or hurts remains open. We crossed AI partnership (one versus two) with behavioral formation (calibrated to average human behavior versus customized by the participant) in a brainstorming experiment ($N$=168) with human-human dyads as reference. Two-AI rooms posted more ideas to the shared board, but human-authored ideas dropped substantially. With one AI partner, formation mattered: humans paired with an average-calibrated AI posted more than any other condition. With two, this effect vanished. Humans continued talking but converted fewer ideas into board posts. AI social talk predicted more human posts, while AI posting volume predicted fewer. AI presence increased global diversity of human-authored ideas, but only a second AI increased within-session differentiation. The number of AI partners and their formation can reshape what the human contributes; single-agent results do not generalize to multi-agent teams.

all_scored.title: Generalist Action Critic: Harnessing Frontier Models in Autonomous Driving
all_scored.summary: Frontier models have demonstrated remarkable general-purpose reasoning capabilities, opening new possibilities for intelligent decision making in the physical world. In autonomous driving, many recent approaches seek to leverage these capabilities through additional adaptation for action output, particularly in scenarios where existing models underperform. We introduce Generalist Action Critic (GAC), a zero-shot framework that combines frontier models' general-purpose reasoning with the planning competence of specialized driving models through an inference-time harness. In GAC, specialized planners generate multiple candidate trajectories and make an initial selection, while a frozen frontier model serves as an action critic that assesses the selected trajectory against scene evidence and either retains it or reselects from the available candidates. The harness combines camera images with spatial overlays, provides driving context and reasoning principles through textual instructions, and regulates the information available at each stage to support trajectory assessment and reselection. On HUGSIM, GAC raises DrivoR's HD-Score to 43.2, achieving state-of-the-art performance among methods trained without additional simulation data. GAC also consistently improves closed-loop driving safety across three planners, with relative HD-Score gains of up to 32.1%. Experiments on NAVSIM v1 further reveal how GAC improves planning performance by correcting up to 52.13% of eligible unsafe trajectory selections while introducing new failures in only 0.67% of originally high-quality selections. These results demonstrate the potential of harnessing frontier models to improve driving safety through inference-time cooperation with specialized planners.
all_scored.reason: reasoning: reasoning; planning_and_action: planning, trajectory, decision making; downranked: driving, autonomous driving

all_scored.title: ROSWORLD: When Digital Task Competence Meets Physical Execution
all_scored.summary: Computer-use agents now solve most desktop tasks through direct software input, but a robot using the same computer must turn GUI knowledge into physical contact with a keyboard and mouse. We introduce ROSWorld, a benchmark that couples a physically simulated robot workstation to a live OSWorld desktop, so that a robot and a desktop agent pursue the same goals under the same official evaluators. The evaluated model receives observations only from the workstation camera views and operates the peripherals through either a single-arm rigid probe or dual-arm dexterous hands. Across five frontier models and 40 tasks in ten applications, models that complete 31-39 tasks on the desktop complete at most 23 with the probe and 28 with the hands. Paired trajectory analysis shows that models adapt their interaction strategies toward keyboard input, yet physical execution frequently fails through missed presses, incorrect targets, and unintended contacts. ROSWorld makes the gap between knowing what to do on a computer and physically doing it measurable.

all_scored.title: Ego2Ego: Generative Visual Perspective Taking Across Collaborators
all_scored.summary: Visual perspective taking, the ability to infer what another person sees from their position, is fundamental to human collaboration. However, prior works reduced perspective taking to state estimation, geometric reconstruction, or discrete question answering, whereas existing cross-view video generation methods either inferred the target view from the input video alone or required an external camera that observes the target person. We introduce generative visual perspective taking: Given an ego person's egocentric video, a scene point cloud, and a collaborator's camera trajectory, the task is to generate the continuous egocentric video from the collaborator's perspective. This task is challenging given extreme viewpoint shifts, dynamic occlusions, and sparse visual overlap. We address these challenges with Ego2Ego -- a set of backbone-agnostic geometric modules that provide a pretrained video diffusion model with the 3D scene geometry shared by both interactants. Ego2Ego renders dense, temporally consistent scene coordinate maps into every view as a shared spatial reference, aligns cross-view tokens in 3D ray space through relative geometric attention, and recovers regions outside the ego person's current view from the ego person's visual memory. Experiments on the CoMind dataset across three video diffusion backbones show that Ego2Ego consistently improves visual quality, Level-2 scene layout accuracy, and collaborator motion, outperforming state-of-the-art cross-view video generation baselines on every backbone. By generating the collaborator's egocentric video more accurately, Ego2Ego brings visual perspective taking to human-robot collaboration, where it can help infer what a human collaborator sees and does, and can turn single-person recordings into synchronised multi-perspective videos for robot learning.

all_scored.title: GGDriver: Glance at What Is Shared, Gaze at What Differs for Perception-Free Planning
all_scored.summary: A planner deciding whether to turn left or continue straight needs to inspect different parts of the scene for each maneuver. Yet many end-to-end driving planners evaluate every candidate trajectory against the same compressed scene representation. We let each candidate select the visual evidence used to refine and score it. A global glance first produces trajectory hypotheses from shared scene features. We then project a corridor around each trajectory into the camera views and use the resulting mask to attend to patch features at the backbone's native resolution. After refinement, the scorer projects each final proposal again and ranks it using evidence along its own path. This geometric selection requires only the predicted trajectory and camera calibration. On three planners with different scene representations (learned registers, a perception-supervised bird's-eye-view grid, and a coarse image-token grid), adding this gaze improves planning scores. In ablations, path-aligned patches outperform both a matched number of randomly selected patches and attention over all patches. Using the gaze for ranking yields larger gains than using it for refinement alone. With a ViT-S backbone and no perception labels, GGDriver achieves a rater feedback score of 8.110 on the WOD-E2E test set, 94.2 PDMS on NAVSIM-v1, 48.6 EPDMS on NAVSIM-v2, and a closed-loop Driving Score of 72.18 on Bench2Drive.

all_scored.title: Coherence by Construction: Synthesizing CTI Knowledge Graphs and the Formal Limits of Coherence Validation
all_scored.summary: Synthesizing relational training data such as knowledge graphs with a large language model typically emits structured objects one at a time, which keeps each object valid but leaves the relationships between them ungrounded. We study an alternative paradigm, generation by simulation: rather than describing a relational artifact, we simulate a process that produces it and take the artifact to be its causal record. Language-model agents propose intent and a deterministic referee resolves outcomes against an explicit world model, so a relation is emitted only when the event it represents occurs, making coherence a property of construction. We instantiate the paradigm for cyber threat intelligence knowledge graphs in the STIX 2.1 standard with three engines, among them an evolutionary engine applying language-model genetic operators to structured graph genomes, sharing a deterministic compiler that makes malformed and dangling output unrepresentable. We prove referential closure, causal grounding, and identifier stability, an ablation localizes each to the referee and world model rather than the policy, and two independent LLM judges reproduce the rubric's engine ranking. Our central result is cautionary, and we prove it: a validator reading any graph feature set a structure-matched random graph can reproduce is uninformative about coherence for a coherence-by-construction generator. Using Erdős-Rényi controls we realize the theorem four times, as structural separation, embedding transfer, inductive link prediction, and real-data augmentation each reward a triviality rather than coherence; we give the mechanism behind each and the conditions a valid benchmark must meet.

all_scored.title: Non-penetrating World Models
all_scored.summary: We study a new problem of preventing object penetration in interactive video world models. To understand how existing models handle this, we introduce NoPeBench, a benchmark that evaluates how world models respond to physical obstacles. Our evaluation reveals that none of the open-source models can reliably prevent such failures. Surprisingly, however, these models already encode the information needed to predict such violations. We find that the hidden states of diffusion transformers (DiTs) can predict whether a candidate action will penetrate an obstacle. Building on this, we introduce NoPeWorld, a lightweight framework that detects and prevents penetration. Specifically, we train a small prediction head on top of a frozen DiT's hidden states to read out if a candidate action is safe or not. Unsafe actions are then replaced with safe ones that best preserve the original intent. Despite its simplicity, NoPeWorld substantially reduces the physical violation rate, averaged over six video world models, from 74% to 16%. Remarkably, our method shows zero-shot generalization to open-domain imagery, third-person viewpoints, and moving obstacles. We publicly release our code, the NoPeBench benchmark, and model weights. Project Page: https://nopeworld.github.io .

all_scored.title: Auditable Financial Knowledge Graphs: Schema-Driven Construction and Intrinsic Quality Evaluation
all_scored.summary: Financial documents combine narrative disclosures, accounting metrics, corporate structures, management commentary, and time-dependent facts, making them difficult to represent using conventional chunk-based retrieval-augmented generation systems. This paper presents an auditable, schema-driven methodology for constructing temporal financial knowledge graphs from page-delimited documents parsed using a general purpose document intelligence service. Overlapping document windows undergo phased large language model extraction of structural entities, quantitative observations, and domain-specific relationships. Candidate graph elements are validated against predefined schemas and consolidated through scope-aware exact, normalized, fuzzy, embedding-based, and LLM-assisted entity resolution. Temporal merge constraints, deterministic edge deduplication, conflict-aware property management, and fine-grained provenance preserve issuer identity, reporting-period validity, and traceability to source evidence. The contributions of this work comprise the proposed methodology for financial knowledge graph construction, the creation of an evidence-grounded temporal knowledge graph from heterogeneous financial documents, and an intrinsic framework for evaluating the quality of the resulting graph. The evaluation framework assesses seven weighted dimensions, two hard validation gates, and structural diagnostics. By separating graph-quality assessment from downstream retrieval and answer generation, the framework supports systematic diagnosis and iterative refinement of the constructed graph.

all_scored.title: Redesigning Neural Networks to Not be Confidently Wrong even to Strong Adversarial Attacks
all_scored.summary: Early deep learning models attempted to simulate visual perception using a neural hierarchy that alternated between two types of layer: one modelled on cortical simple cells (that was designed to increase selectivity), and one modelled on cortical complex cells (that aimed to increase tolerance). We show that such a neural network (NN) architecture, when implemented with novel components that are better able to learn selective and tolerant representations, is capable of accurate and robust image classification and improved alignment between the behaviour of the model and the perceptual abilities of humans. Firstly, the proposed models are shallow, fewer than ten layer-pairs, which is more consistent with the rapid feedforward object categorisation performed by the biological visual system. Secondly, they are far less prone to producing classification predictions with high confidence for samples from unknown classes or for image consisting of pure noise, and hence, like humans are not easily fooled into perceiving objects that are not present in the image. Thirdly, for the proposed NNs adversarial samples cause predictions with low confidence, enabling them to be accurately identified. In contrast to humans, our networks still do not correctly classify adversarial samples. However, the behaviour of our networks is a significant step towards human-like behaviour compared to standard DNNs that produce highly confident, but incorrect, classification predictions for adversarial samples. The increased robustness to adversarial and unknown samples is achieved while maintaining competitive performance in terms of generalisation to novel samples from the training categories. This enables models of this type to be competitive with state-of-the-art DNNs across multiple different evaluation metrics and benchmark tasks.

all_scored.title: A Benchmark Protocol and Fairness Analysis Towards Open-Set EEG Seizure Type Classification
all_scored.summary: Automated EEG seizure type classification systems are typically trained and evaluated under the closed-set assumption, where all seizure types encountered at deployment are seen during training. In clinical practice, this assumption fails: patients present with rare or atypical seizure types that fall outside the training label space, and a system that forces a wrong label is worse than one that abstains. We introduce the first open-set recognition protocol for EEG seizure type classification on the Temple University Hospital Seizure Corpus (TUSZ v2.0.3), defining known and unknown classes using the clinical taxonomy itself: seizure types with sufficient subject representation (at least 12 subjects) form the known set, and rare types form the unknown set. We evaluate seven post-hoc open-set scorers (MSP, MaxLogit, energy, Mahalanobis, kNN, GHOST, and COSTARR) applied to a partially fine-tuned EEG Foundation Model (EFM), using a subject-disjoint leave-one-class-out (LOCO) protocol over three seeds that tests whether methods can detect seizure types excluded from fine-tuning. On true unknown classes, the best scorer (Mahalanobis) reaches a mean AUROC of 0.66, and differences among the top scorers are within seed-to-seed variation. Held-out known seizure types from unseen subjects are detected only slightly above chance (AUROC 0.54-0.58 for all scorers). Per-subject rejection rates are highly uneven for all scorers, and GHOST does not significantly improve per-subject fairness over energy scoring (two-sided Wilcoxon signed-rank, p >= 0.25). We release the protocol, subject splits, and code as an initial baseline; our results indicate that open-set seizure type recognition remains a hard, open problem.

all_scored.title: AutoOntologyBench: A Task-Grounded Benchmark for Agentic Knowledge Engineering
all_scored.summary: Foundation-model agents are increasingly extending beyond software engineering (SWE) into autonomous scientific research, where acquiring and integrating domain knowledge remains a critical challenge. Recent industrial advances have increasingly adopted knowledge graphs and ontology-based semantic layers to organize heterogeneous knowledge into reusable representations. We ask: Can autonomous agents construct ontologies that help them solve real tasks, and do they offer measurable benefits over alternative knowledge representations? Existing benchmarks evaluate ontology correctness or agent task success in isolation, leaving the value of autonomously acquired knowledge unresolved. We therefore introduce AutoOntologyBench, a task-grounded benchmark comprising 19,947 audited tasks grounded in 18 real-world knowledge sources across 7 domains, with source-native verification. Spanning Application, Repair, Organization, and Construction, AutoOntologyBench compares nine frontier-model agents under matched knowledge representations. Layered on retrieval, agent-built ontologies add 6.1 points of task success, yet trail an expert-derived reference by 13.0, identifying autonomous knowledge acquisition as the bottleneck to scalable scientific research. Code and resources are available at https://github.com/VinyehShaw/AutoOntologyBench.

all_scored.title: Circular Predictive Coding Unlocks Effective Depth
all_scored.summary: Predictive coding networks perform credit assignment through an energy minimization process. Despite their ability to train models with arbitrary network topologies, they have mostly been used to train feedforward architectures to match the performance of backpropagation. However, they fail to do so when the models become too deep, because error signals become unstable or vanish as they travel through many layers. We address this limitation with circular networks, which get their depth directly from the energy minimization, rather than from stacking layers. Formally, we prove that convergence to an equilibrium of the energy functional of a circular predictive coding network approximates the fixed-point iteration process of a deep equilibrium model, showing that circularity alone suffices to unlock effective depth. Empirically, we show that circular models (i) outperform other predictive coding models of the same size on image classification tasks, matching the accuracy of state-of-the-art predictive coding ResNets and VGG networks despite having substantially fewer parameters; (ii) solve constraint satisfaction problems that require many steps of iterative reasoning, a task not feasible with feedforward models at all, reaching 99.3% test accuracy on Sudoku-hard via nested energy minimization loops; and (iii) scale to autoregressive language modeling by training a circular transformer on TinyStories and WikiText-103, before out of reach for predictive coding models. These results have direct implications for physical neural networks, where computational depth can be traded for recursion on a fixed-size circuit.

all_scored.title: Adapting AI Weather Foundation Models to a Changing Climate
all_scored.summary: AI weather foundation models learn from historical archives, while the climate distribution encountered during deployment continues to evolve. This growing model--climate mismatch motivates continual adaptation without repeated full-model retraining, but the structure of weather forecast errors determines how such adaptation should be performed. We develop an online adaptation framework that exploits two complementary error structures: geographically persistent biases and flow-dependent errors that vary with the atmospheric state. Analysis of Aurora-1.3B reveals strongly concentrated forecast-loss sensitivity in its decoder, motivating flow-dependent corrections within fixed low-dimensional sensitivity subspaces. A residual memory tracks persistent errors remaining after this correction, while a variable-wise online gate controls the contribution of the persistent component. We evaluate Aurora-1.3B using ERA5 from 1959--1968 for offline initialization and a strictly chronological 1969--2022 stream for online evaluation, with updates restricted to previously available verification targets. For 2-metre temperature, distributional departure from the historical reference, measured directly from ERA5, is associated with larger frozen-model errors and greater adaptation gains, while the adapted model maintains more stable skill across evaluation periods. Across 69 output fields and five lead times from 6 to 72 hours, our method reduces MSE and MAE by 6.90\% and 6.45\%, respectively, relative to $δ$-Adapter, the strongest of six online adaptation baselines.

all_scored.title: TITAN: DRL-Based Dynamic Scheduling and Resource Allocation for Tactile Internet
all_scored.summary: Tactile Internet (TI) applications require ultra-reliable, low-latency tactile communication alongside video traffic. However, tactile Quality of Service (QoS) requirements vary with the interaction context, making fixed resource allocation inefficient. In this paper, we propose TITAN (Two-Timescale Integrated Tactile Internet over 5G Access Networks), a dynamic scheduling and resource allocation (SRA) scheme. TITAN receives time-varying tactile QoS profiles from a higher-layer module and adapts SRA to the current QoS profile and network state. A deep reinforcement learning-based agent splits the available network bandwidth between tactile and video streams at a slow timescale, while a fast-timescale scheduler allocates resource blocks among active user equipment. Through simulations, we show that TITAN simultaneously satisfies both tactile and video QoS targets and achieves a performance gain of 7.64 percentage points (pp) in the joint satisfaction rate over the best-performing static SRA baseline.

all_scored.title: Communication-constrained multiagent risk estimation: a simulation benchmark for adult sore throat
all_scored.summary: Distributed predictive agents may need to approach a shared estimate under limited, unreliable communication. We evaluated classical symmetric pairwise gossip among five agents initialized from frozen calibrated predictions in a synthetic adult sore-throat benchmark. Ninety runs across three fixed generator families supplied 270,000 underlying test encounters, each observed through four missingness views. Complete, ring and star graphs were compared at eight interaction budgets and transaction failure probabilities of 0, 0.2 and 0.5. The coordination extension was designed after inspection of the predictive benchmark and is exploratory. Outcomes were disagreement around the conserved arithmetic mean and its exact decomposition of mean-agent Brier error. In the base view at eight attempted pairs and 0.2 failure, disagreement variance was 0.000109 for the complete graph, 0.000134 for the ring and 0.000175 for the star. The paired complete-minus-ring difference was -0.000024 (95% Monte Carlo interval -0.000030 to -0.000019). The centralized mean had base Brier 0.069781, compared with 0.069368 for Kumo alone. Agreement therefore does not establish superiority to the strongest individual predictor. Code, fixed probability inputs and results support replay without model refitting. The study quantifies finite-budget coordination under specified simulation assumptions; it proposes no new gossip algorithm and establishes no clinical accuracy or utility.

all_scored.title: Cleave: Severing Guardrails and Auditing Spectral Coupling in Open-Weight LLMs
all_scored.summary: Open-weight Large Language Models (LLMs) are widely downloaded for their strong coding and reasoning capabilities and deployed locally beyond the provider's control. To prevent misuse, developers embed safety guardrails into these models before release. However, we find that these guardrails rely on the residual writing weights to trigger refusals. Based on this insight, we propose Cleave, a training-free attack that directly edits these weights to remove safety restrictions while preserving general capabilities. With Cleave, malicious users can either remove all guardrails or selectively lift only cybersecurity restrictions. Because this selective removal retains up to a 99% refusal rate on other harmful requests and avoids weight rank collapse, it evades both behavioral spot-checks and static weight audits. Across five open-weight LLMs from 7B to 320B parameters, Cleave achieves up to a 67.97% attack success rate on seven safety benchmarks, substantially outperforming existing white-box baselines. On 356 cybersecurity tasks and 15 live vulnerable services, it further boosts executable exploit generation by up to 24.0 times and compromises up to 66.7% of the targets. To counter this threat, we propose a dual-stage defense that combines pre-release subspace diagnostics with post-release weight-coupling audits, achieving 100% detection recall at a 1% false-positive rate.

all_scored.title: Evidence sufficiency assessment enables cost-effective review allocation in on-premise clinical AI agents
all_scored.summary: On-premise clinical AI agents must auto-accept high-confidence diagnoses, deferring others to clinician review, yet token probabilities and self-reported confidence miss errors, while more reliable five-run consistency incurs fivefold compute. We propose training-free decision-point evidence sufficiency assessment and a three-tier sequential triage protocol. Masking reasoning and diagnosis, the same 4B model scores sufficiency from objective evidence via prior-debiased probabilities over five ordered levels. Calibration freezes a nominal top-50% threshold, selecting single-run, five-run consistency, or full-deferral tiers by whether the one-sided 95% Wilson lower confidence bound of pass rate among accepted cases meets the 95% clinical target line. Across 1,605 MIRA-v2, CDM, VivaBench, and in-hospital liver malignancy primary cohort cases, MIRA-v2 single-run top-50% pass rate reached 98.91%, matching five-run consistency, saving ~80% compute; CDM achieved 96.00% test attainment by escalating to the five-run consistency tier; cross-specialty, missing-imaging, and combined enriched cohorts entered the full-deferral tier, capping calibration false-certification rate at 0.00%-3.50%.

all_scored.title: WePM: Hierarchical Conflict Reconciliation for Unified MLLMs
all_scored.summary: Bringing multimodal intelligence from the cloud to users' devices keeps sensitive data local and reduces inference cost, but deploying a specialized model per capability duplicates vision-language capacity under tight memory and compute budgets. We formalize heterogeneous capability density (HCD), measuring how broadly and effectively a model serves heterogeneous task families per unit of resident inference memory. High HCD across representation, generation, and decision raises two challenges: these capabilities need visual evidence at different spatial granularities under a fixed token budget, and separately collected task corpora yield conflicting updates to shared parameters, while cross-task paired supervision is costly and ambiguous for open-ended inputs. We present WePM, a family of pocket models unifying representation, generation, and decision within one vision-language backbone. Multi-Granularity Visual Budgeting (MGVB) allocates a fixed visual-token budget across global, regional, and fine-grained banks; Unified Listwise Knowledge Distillation (ULKD) enriches separately collected data with soft teacher guidance, avoiding cross-task paired annotation; Stable and Efficient Multitask Optimization (SEMO) regulates each task's contribution through explicit loss weights and exposure schedules, with sequential gradient accumulation under memory constraints. In the joint representation-generation setting, WePM outperforms all baselines across five evaluation groups, raising the Joint score from 38.15 to 52.74. In single-task evaluation, WePM-4B attains the best average score over 30 embedding, 39 generation, and seven typed-decision benchmarks (72.86, 62.41, 61.11). Against the separate-model stack with the highest HCD, WePM achieves slightly higher balanced performance with 61.9% less resident weight memory, a 2.64-fold higher HCD.

all_scored.title: Unimodal Shortcuts and Joint Scene-Intent Dependence in Vision-Language Safety Representations
all_scored.summary: The safety of a request to a vision-language model often depends on the image: asking how to serve a dish is harmless for fresh food and harmful for spoiled food. High accuracy on situational safety benchmarks does not tell us whether a model's safety representation encodes both the scene and the user's intent, because a benchmark can often be solved from one modality alone. Studying frozen vision-language safety representations, we audit five public situational benchmarks and find that each admits a unimodal shortcut: images alone predict the labels, and on same-image prompt pairs a probe that never sees the photograph reaches 0.9645 AUROC. We therefore build a controlled evaluation that crosses safe and hazardous scenes with observation and action requests, so that no single-modality rule can exceed 0.500 group-ranking accuracy. On this control, linear probes on intermediate states of Qwen3-VL-8B and SmolVLM2-2.2B reach 0.958 and 0.930, showing that the scene-intent conjunction is linearly decodable; concatenating separately encoded image and text states already recovers most of this signal, so decodability is not evidence of a fusion mechanism. The same probes screen cheaply but generalize poorly to unseen images and other benchmarks. Reliable multimodal safety evaluation therefore needs controls that rule out unimodal shortcuts before accuracy is read as evidence of joint understanding.

all_scored.title: DermKG: A Concept-Centric Knowledge Graph for Interpretable Skin Disease Diagnosis from Dermatological Morphology
all_scored.summary: Dermatologists describe lesions with a standardized morphological lexicon, which makes concept-based models attractive for interpretable skin disease diagnosis. How much diagnostic information these concepts actually carry, however, is rarely quantified. We present DermKG, a concept-centric knowledge graph built on the expert-annotated SkinCon subset of Fitzpatrick17k (3,230 images, 48 concepts, 113 diseases). DermKG has 3,452 nodes of 8 types and 19,365 edges of 11 relation types, and encodes disease concept profiles, concept co-occurrence, a three-level diagnostic hierarchy, and 20 clinical morphology rules, all of which are supported by the training data (15 strong, 5 moderate). An information-ceiling analysis shows that the 3,230 lesions collapse onto only 813 distinct concept vectors, bounding concept-only top-1 accuracy at 38.9\% for diseases and 77.6\% for the nine categories. Within this bound, DermKG-Net, a graph neural network that scores lesions against disease prototypes and aggregates them along the hierarchy, raises category-level balanced accuracy from 0.257 to 0.411 over the strongest of 11 baselines (paired bootstrap difference $+0.150$, 95\% CI $[0.073, 0.231]$) and more than doubles minority-category recall. Ablations show that most of this gain comes from the hierarchical prototype objective, with a smaller contribution from graph structure. DermKG further yields rule-based reasoning chains and concept-level explanations for individual predictions.

all_scored.title: Error-Corrected Physics-Informed Neural Operator for Optimal Control of Unmanned Aerial Vehicles under Uncertainty
all_scored.summary: We solve open-loop optimal control problems under parametric uncertainty using a physics-informed DeepONet that returns trajectories for all sampled scenarios in one evaluation. Trained only on the residual at generic controls, the operator is reused across targets and horizons. Because a gradient-based optimizer exploits surrogate errors, we correct the prediction by one Newton step on the dynamics, computed for all scenarios and times by one parallel scan. The corrected state has a second-order error bounded by the residual alone, and the corrected cost is honest for every control up to the sampling error. On a fixed-wing UAV benchmark, the corrected operator matches the accuracy of a batched Adam solver and an Ipopt solver at equal sample size and is 8 times faster than the Adam solver on the same GPU at a few hundred scenarios and 15 times faster than Ipopt on a CPU.

all_scored.title: NavTTT: Adaptive Parametric Memory via Hierarchical Test-Time Training for Vision-and-Language Navigation
all_scored.summary: Vision-and-language navigation (VLN) demands that agents accumulate and reason over streaming visual observations throughout long navigation episodes. Existing approaches struggle to maintain long-term history, constrained by the finite context capacity of transformer architectures. To solve the problem, fast-weight test-time training (TTT) provides a mechanism for encoding streaming observations into an evolving parameter state. However, existing TTT does not distinguish informative observations from repetitive visual content, allowing redundant tokens to interfere with the retention of information needed for subsequent decisions. We propose Navigation-Conditioned Test-Time Training (NavTTT), which introduces adaptive memory formation and hierarchical memory integration for vision-and-language navigation. NavTTT leverages global navigation context to prioritize informative visual evidence and integrates language instructions with spatial information to construct spatially grounded memory representations. Episode-local nonlinear fast weights store these representations as Adaptive Parametric Memory (APM), preserving history beyond the visual context for later decisions. To reduce cross-layer coupling in memory formation, NavTTT maintains independent fast-weight memories across multiple decoder depths. This decoupled design prevents errors or biases from spreading across different memory levels. Meanwhile, it enables shared historical information to be independently represented at various levels of abstraction. Experiments demonstrate strong navigation performance on VLN-CE benchmarks and effective instruction following on a real robot.

all_scored.title: What Does Matching a Human Intervention Effect Establish? Benchmark Checks for LLM Simulations
all_scored.summary: LLM simulations are validated by equivalence with human effects, yet a zero reference passes whenever the human 90 percent interval lies inside the margin, as the human benchmark shows before simulation. When the zero reference fails, planned precision gives independent simulations the margin up to which passing is a 5 percent test of response. In an exploratory 70-experiment reanalysis, 72 percent of GPT-4's $\pm$0.20 SD passes were zero-reference passes; GPT-4 passed 16 contrasts the zero reference failed (1.58 expected without response). In a preregistered audit, Claude Sonnet 5.5 passed three intention targets, all zero-reference passes, and the registered belief-gradient control; norm beliefs changed 0.065 SD against humans' 0.351 (zero-reference check added after unblinding; norm beliefs emphasized after inspection). Registered tests detected no overestimation; average-effect intervals excluded overestimation above 0.08 SD. A group audit's precision floor is 1.33 facts against a 2.9-fact effect. Report the zero-reference threshold beside every equivalence decision.

all_scored.title: HumanoidPose: Monocular 3D Pose Estimation for Humanoid Robots
all_scored.summary: As humanoid robots increasingly enter real-world environments, recovering their 3D whole-body pose from monocular imagery is becoming increasingly important for external state perception, motion analysis, and robot learning. However, Humanoid Robot Pose Estimation (HRPE) lies at the intersection of conventional Robot Pose Estimation (RPE) and Human Pose Estimation (HPE), while not being fully addressed by either paradigm: RPE primarily focuses on non-humanoid robots, particularly fixed-base manipulators, whereas HPE is built upon human-specific skeletal topologies, body models, and motion priors. Despite recent progress in humanoid 2D keypoint detection and HPE adaptation, humanoid-native 3D pose recovery remains insufficiently studied, and a dedicated benchmark with suitable training data and evaluation protocols is still lacking. To address this gap, we introduce Humanoids, a benchmark for monocular 3D humanoid robot pose estimation, and propose HumanoidPose, a framework for this task. Humanoids provides synthetic 3D supervision across diverse humanoid embodiments, manually annotated real-world 2D data, and real-world RGB sequences paired with robot states for 3D evaluation on a physical Roban humanoid. HumanoidPose combines human-inspired visual perception with robot articulation modeling and explicit kinematic grounding. Experiments on Humanoids and the DHRP-H1 benchmark demonstrate strong performance in articulation recovery and 3D pose estimation, including zero-shot transfer to real-world 2D and 3D evaluation. Ablation studies further show the contribution of robot-native articulation modeling and explicit kinematic grounding. The dataset and code will be publicly released to support future research in the community.

all_scored.title: Learning Adaptive Defense Strategies: Fine-Tuned LLMs for Network Security Games under Network Mobility
all_scored.summary: Large language models(LLM) show promise for strategic reasoning, yet their ability to compute game-theoretic equilibria under dynamic conditions remains largely unexplored. This work investigates whether fine-tuned LLMs can serve as solver-free surrogates for online equilibrium computation in honeypot allocation, a setting in which network mobility continuously reshapes the underlying attack graph and forces repeated re-solving of a two-player zero-sum game. We construct a dataset of 270 security games on networks of 8--25 nodes with solver-grounded equilibrium labels, and evaluate four classes of predictor over 1{,}524 held-out mobility events: non-learned baselines, six open-weight architectures evaluated zero-shot, the same six after LoRA fine-tuning, and four proprietary models as an external reference point. Predictions are scored without post-hoc repair against exact game-theoretic criteria: exploitability against an optimal attacker best-response, equilibrium support accuracy, and distributional distance. Fine-tuning reduces exploitability across every architecture, and fine-tuned open-weight models of modest size outperform every zero-shot predictor, including proprietary ones; no zero-shot model at any tier reaches the floor set by uniform allocation. Stratifying by mobility type exposes a qualitative shift that aggregate metrics conceal: zero-shot models do not condition on whether a departing node lies on an attack path, while fine-tuned models recover this distinction. We further find that validation loss is negatively rank-correlated with task performance, and that output validity, rather than predictive accuracy, is the binding constraint on further progress.

all_scored.title: GaLF-ST: Gaussian Latent Fields for Spatial Transcriptomics Reconstruction
all_scored.summary: Spatial transcriptomics (ST) measures gene expression at known tissue locations to reveal tissue organization and cellular function. Expression prediction requires modeling both local spatial relationships and associations among genes. Existing methods typically model expression using coordinate networks without explicit spatial parameterization. To address limited spatial sampling and sparse expression observations of ST, some methods firstly fit intermediate embeddings and then train expression predictors, but a latent representation suited to expression reconstruction may be difficult to predict from spatial coordinates. The two training stages can impose different demands on the latent representation. In this paper, we propose GaLF-ST, a Gaussian latent field method in which learnable Gaussian centers and anisotropic covariances determine the weights of latent vectors at each location. A shared nonlinear decoder maps their weighted average to multigene expression. In GaLF-ST, observed expression error jointly updates the Gaussian geometry, latent vectors, and decoder parameters. We further establish a unified benchmark across seven dataset groups and three held-out fractions, comparing GaLF-ST with four representative methods using the same locations, splits, gene panels, and scoring rules. Across tissues and observation densities, GaLF-ST achieves leading overall reconstruction performance, recovering spatial gene expression patterns and preserving tissue domains from limited observations while substantially reducing runtime and GPU memory usage.

all_scored.title: Dynamic Memory-enhanced Pattern Relevance Prediction for Long-tailed Graph Classification
all_scored.summary: Long-tailed graph classification (LTGC) is common in real-world graph datasets, where a few large head graphs provide rich structural information while many smaller tail graphs offer fewer structural cues, making it harder to learn discriminative representations for tail graphs. To address this size-based imbalance, we propose Dynamic Memory-enhanced Pattern Relevance Prediction (DMPRP), which transfers structural patterns from head graphs to tail graphs. Given a graph representation as a query, a dynamic expert memory module inspired by Knowledge-diverse Experts (KDEX) generates a residual vector that augments the original representation. We train the module using co-occurrence triplets sampled from head graphs at the node, rooted subgraph, and random-walk neighborhood levels. Experiments on five graph classification benchmarks show that DMPRP improves tail performance, and ablation studies show that both the expert module and random-walk supervision contribute to these gains. A controlled experiment on PTC further examines pattern transfer when smaller graphs are denser than larger ones. Our code is available at https://anonymous.4open.science/r/DMPRP-73A5.

all_scored.title: ORION: Exact Canonical-State Supervision for Systematic Generalization in Transformers
all_scored.summary: Autoregressive Transformers generally fail on out-of-distribution reasoning due to two primary reasons: positional corruption over long sequences and structural state drift across deep execution steps. We introduce ORION, a framework that supervises exact canonical execution states via auxiliary heads to anchor latent trajectories to valid computational manifolds. Across Folding, GridShift, and CLRS-30, a pre-registered 2 x 2 factorial shows that RoPE and ORION address orthogonal axes. RoPE recovers length extrapolation (59.8%), while ORION recovers depth extrapolation (66.7%). Moreover, their combination complementarily achieves strict additive gain in joint length-depth extrapolation, while either method alone offers near satisfactory results. Negative controls confirm that the gain depends strictly on exact canonical alignment; hashed state statistics fail to constrain depth extrapolation.

all_scored.title: Rethinking Cross-Sensor Domain Adaptation for Bridge Point Cloud Semantic Segmentation
all_scored.summary: Segmentation models for bridge point clouds lose accuracy when trained on terrestrial laser scanning (TLS) data and applied to mobile laser scanning (MLS) data. This study re-examines the SemanticBridge TLS-to-MLS protocol to determine how sampling density, surface roughness, color, and acquisition viewpoint are expressed in the 8-cm sparse-voxel representation, and how adaptation gains depend on source-model convergence. Using one sparse-convolution U-Net, we combine raw-point statistics with controlled input perturbations and compare adaptive batch normalization, entropy minimization, Mean Teacher, and confidence-filtered self-training under 100- and 300-epoch schedules. TLS and MLS have similar nearest-neighbor spacing after preprocessing (12.08 and 12.02 mm), and a 4-mm perturbation of TLS points changes voxel occupancy by only 4.4%. Color distributions differ systematically, but zeroing color on identical voxels changes target mean intersection over union (mIoU) by only +0.02, and by +0.06 after the color augmentation is scale-corrected. The sensors also observe different portions of the bridge, yielding different class proportions. A 300-epoch source-only model obtains 57.80 mIoU on the paired-bridge protocol. Confidence-filtered self-training improves the 100-epoch baseline, but from a converged model it changes target mIoU by -0.97 (source-selected checkpoints) and -2.44 (final-50-epoch means). Repeated evaluation (standard deviation 0.27-0.64) and seed variation (1.88 across three seeds) are comparable to several method differences. Adaptation results on this benchmark therefore depend on representation scale, source-model convergence, and evaluation variability.

all_scored.title: NightmareDiscourseBench: A Benchmark Dataset for Fictional Direct Discourse Identification Pipelines
all_scored.summary: In this paper we introduce a new benchmark dataset, NightmareDiscourseBench, for testing NLP pipelines that identify forms of direct discourse in English-language fiction. We first review existing publicly available benchmarks (providing summary statistics and reviewing available metadata) for this task, identifying theoretical inconsistency and exclusive focus on speech as primary issues in this domain. We then overview our narrative theory-based framework for classifying and evaluating different forms of direct discourse, and finally describe NightmareDiscourseBench, a new benchmark test set of 12 text samples accompanied by metadata pertinent to the task of direct discourse identification.

all_scored.title: Privacy Protection in Self-Evolving Personal Agents: Persistent Memory and Cross-Carrier Transfer
all_scored.summary: Personal agents carry private experience into later decisions through persistent memory. This thematic survey compares memory admission, maintenance, release, and withdrawal by protected change, observer, and validation setting. Direct evidence in the screened corpus comes from controlled memory workflows. Three worked scenarios follow one private fact through booking, feedback-driven learning, and withdrawal. We show when prompt revision and memory reads compose, when skills inherit a private head's bound, and why reader non-use does not establish cleanup of learned state. Diagnostic experiments measure the utility costs of wider label protection and broad memory deletion, and test how missing lineage obscures descendants.

all_scored.title: Beyond Prompt Heuristics: Assessing Child Safety Alignment in LLMs
all_scored.summary: Child-safety taxonomies typically characterize safety risks through a predefined set of harm categories, and existing evaluations largely operationalize these categories using prompts that explicitly invoke them. However, child-safety considerations can also arise in seemingly benign requests that lack recognizable harm-category cues. We therefore investigate how child-safety alignment generalizes to such settings. Across six models, we find considerably higher misalignment rates on requests without recognizable harm-category cues than on those containing such cues (80.0, 54.0, and 48.4 percentage-point gaps for Qwen3.5-27B, GPT-5.4-mini, and Claude-Haiku-4.5, respectively). Through controlled behavioral and mechanistic analyses, we find that introducing a single harm-associated word reduces misalignment across most models, with mechanistic evidence suggesting that child-safety reasoning may rely in part on lexical and semantic associations with words in the prompt. Our findings motivate evaluations that treat child safety as context-dependent, and not reducible to a fixed set of harm categories.

all_scored.title: Improving the Optimisation Landscape for Particle Mixtures
all_scored.summary: Several methods in statistics and machine learning represent a predictive distribution as an equally weighted mixture of models, or particles, trained via the mixture predictive likelihood. However, we prove that the mixture predictive likelihood is poorly suited to gradient-based optimisation, because it does not identify how the mixture is decomposed across particles, so that a poorly matched particle can be starved of training signal. As a remedy, we study a convex combination between the individual risk, i.e. the average log loss of the individual particles, and the mixture risk. At the particle level, this regularised risk imposes a reverse-KL barrier on the responsibilities of the particles, so that no particle can be starved of training signal. These phenomena are illustrated in two case studies: In the first, a predictively-oriented posterior is computed using mean-field Langevin dynamics, and the numerics are well-behaved only when our regularisation is employed. In the second, ensembles of low-rank adapters are jointly fine-tuned on large language models, across four backbones and eight multiple-choice reasoning benchmarks; direct minimisation of the mixture risk leads to responsibility starvation, whose severity decreases as the competence of the backbone increases, whereas our regularised estimator attains a lower held-out mixture risk on every backbone considered.

all_scored.title: Multi-Tier Edge Triage: Optimizing Latency for Safe Clinical Agents
all_scored.summary: Deploying generative AI agents in enterprise clinical workflows requires enforcing multi-dimensional safety and compliance policies--preventing HIPAA Protected Health Information (PHI) exposure, maintaining clinical scope-of-practice boundaries, ensuring patient-appropriate reading comprehension, and preserving brand integrity--under interactive latency constraints. Synchronous outbound calls to cloud Large Language Model (LLM) judges add substantial network and decoding overhead onto the critical response path. We present Multi-Tier Edge Triage, a safety screening architecture that co-locates a compact Tier-1 sequence classifier on the clinical agent's host server, resolving clear queries in-process without a network round-trip and escalating only ambiguous queries to a Tier-2 cloud LLM judge. To evaluate Tier-1 encoders without length or unigram shortcuts, we construct four length-matched contrastive twin benchmarks seeded from MedSafetyBench, ASQ-PHI, and a synthetic four-mandate clinical assistant policy (Generic HealthCorp). While frozen local encoders match cloud models on structured PHI detection (>= 98.3% accuracy in <= 23.5 ms), they degrade markedly on semantic safety and symmetric-blocklist prompts. However, end-to-end representation fine-tuning closes the multi-policy accuracy gap: a fine-tuned 335M-parameter BGE-Large classifier achieves 98.90% out-of-fold accuracy versus 99.20% for a zero-shot cloud LLM judge (exact McNemar p = 0.648, zero shared errors), 97.8%-98.2% recall, and a 0.0%-0.4% over-refusal rate in 39.0 ms (>14x faster than cloud LLM evaluation on our benchmark host). Per-policy error analysis reveals ceiling local recall on PHI (100.0%), brand (100.0%), and clinical scope (98.7%-99.3%) violations, isolating residual errors to reading-level checks (93.3%-95.3%) and motivating targeted multi-tier escalation.

all_scored.title: Perceive Once, Escalate on Demand: Handing Off Visual KV Memory from Small to Large VLMs
all_scored.summary: An embodied agent cannot afford a large vision-language model (VLM) at every step of a long video, so a cascade runs a small VLM continuously and escalates only uncertain decisions to a large one. Each escalation, however, forces the large model to re-encode a history the small model has already perceived, and this dominates its cost. We present Baton, which hands the large model the small model's visual memory, its key-value (KV) cache over the history. Baton rests on one finding: the large model needs a usable memory, not a faithful copy of its own. A map trained to reproduce the large model's cache matches it most closely, yet brings no gain over the small model alone. Baton instead distills a per-layer linear map, without labels, from the large model's own answers, with the large model encoding only the current frame. Interventions on the map trace the gain to one direction, carried by the middle third of the large model's layers. On RoboMME, Baton beats the small model alone, a pruned or shortened re-watch, and a text memory; as the escalation channel of a cascade it matches re-watching to within about one point at 28-47% less compute, and 8x less per escalation at 64 frames. Its gain grows with the large model, from 8B to 32B, tracks the large model's headroom across eight model pairs from four families, and transfers zero-shot to OpenEQA.

all_scored.title: Your Judge Inherits Your Prompt: In-Context Label Bias in an LLM-as-Judge Is Directional, Not Symmetric
all_scored.summary: LLM-as-judge has become a standard way to score open-ended model outputs, yet the judge is itself a frozen language model steered by a few in-context examples, and such models are known to absorb the label balance of their demonstrations rather than treat them as neutral illustrations. We ask whether this label bias reaches an LLM judge used inside a multimodal (video question answering) evaluation pipeline, and what form it takes. Using a fully frozen generator-judge pipeline, we hold the generated answers fixed and vary only the Yes/No balance of the judge's few-shot examples across four demonstration sets. Each verdict is validated against a two-annotator human consensus on 200 examples per dataset. The judge's acceptance rate stays close to human consensus when its examples are balanced or skewed toward rejection, but jumps sharply (by about 30 points on NExT-QA and 20 on MSVD-QA, with a strongly one-sided error profile) when the examples are skewed toward acceptance; the opposite skew produces no matching drop. The bias is therefore one-directional within the tested range of label ratios. A separate five-draw analysis shows that results from a single example draw are unreliable, varying by up to 18 points, more than any difference between prompting conditions. We conclude that demonstration label bias in an LLM judge is a directional, inflation-only failure mode that can fabricate apparent benchmark gains but not losses, and that it is cheaply avoided by balancing the judge's examples and reporting results averaged over several draws.

all_scored.title: Realistic Robustness Evaluation of Tabular Data Driven Models
all_scored.summary: The increasing adoption of Machine Learning (ML) models in high-stakes applications has raised critical concerns regarding their robustness against adversarial attacks. While extensive research has focused on adversarial example generation in image and text domains, the study of such examples in tabular data remains comparatively limited, despite its widespread use in real-world systems. This work introduces AURORA, a modular, open-source tool for evaluating the robustness of ML models on tabular data classification. It integrates multiple adversarial perturbation methods and evaluation metrics within a unified framework to systematically assess model behavior under adversarial conditions. Central to AURORA is its evaluation report, which focuses on robustness analysis by quantifying performance degradation, comparing the impact of different perturbation strategies, and identifying model vulnerabilities across features and input regions. The report is complemented by visual artifacts that facilitate the interpretability of robustness patterns. Additionally, AURORA incorporates a distance adjustment mechanism that penalizes implausible adversarial samples based on feature-level constraints, ensuring that the robustness assessment remains grounded in realistic perturbations and is therefore more reliable.

all_scored.title: Memorization and Generalization in Generative Models: A Perspective From Energy-based Modeling and Associative Memory
all_scored.summary: Generative models now write working code, produce realistic images, and hold long conversations, yet the mechanisms behind their intelligence still evade our understanding. This thesis explores that puzzle through Associative Memory (AM), in which patterns are stored as energy minima and retrieved through attractor dynamics. Beyond their capacity, AMs form new minima known as spurious states, long regarded as a failure of memory. We argue that this failure is where creativity begins, and that memorization and generalization can coexist as outcomes of one retrieval process. First, we show that diffusion models behave as AMs. With little data, a diffusion model forms a distinct basin of attraction around each training sample. As the data grows, these basins shrink, and spurious states emerge as attractors that blend stored samples yet match none of them. They are the first signs of generative capability. We characterize this transition by measuring the volume, energy, and curvature of these basins across datasets and architectures, including Stable Diffusion. We then turn to language and move beyond the energy-based view of AM. We show that uniform-state discrete diffusion models are AMs capable of retrieving unseen data, with basins of attraction that arise from conditional likelihood maximization alone. As the training set grows, basins around training examples contract while basins around unseen examples expand, until corrupted test sentences are recovered as reliably as training ones. Conditional entropy exposes this coexistence within a single sequence and cheaply diagnoses where a model lies along the transition. Together, these results suggest that AM is a general principle defined by basins of attraction, and that memorization and generalization can coexist within one model. AM thus offers a framework for asking when a generative model recalls and when it creates.

all_scored.title: Depth-Linked Residual Tokens for Multimodal Retrieval and Generation
all_scored.summary: Iterative architectures such as looped language models improve parameter efficiency and reasoning capacity of transformers, yet their sequential backbone iterations introduce substantial computational latency. Conversely, parallelizable learnable special tokens (such as the register tokens in Vision Transformer) enable efficient single-pass inference, but often suffer from the absence of sequential refinement and exhibit redundant representations across tokens. To address these challenges, we introduce Depth-Linked Residual Tokens (DepThink), an efficient framework designed for multimodal retrieval and generation. Operating within a single pre-filling forward pass, DepThink appends a sequence of K learnable residual tokens whose hidden states are coupled through a lightweight, learnable residual recurrence. This mechanism enables each residual token to progressively capture complementary information missed by preceding tokens. Theoretically, we prove that DepThink provides strictly expanded geometric directional reachability over standard learnable tokens and guarantees a provable one-step descent advantage. We evaluate DepThink across multimodal retrieval and generation tasks. DepThink consistently outperforms learnable-token baselines and matches or exceeds looped architectures across dense (2B, 8B) and sparse mixture-of-experts (30B-A3B) backbones under both LoRA and full-parameter fine-tuning, while accelerating training by up to 11.9 and inference by 4.3 over looped architectures.

all_scored.title: Task2Hand: A Contact-Grounded Skill for Parametric Dexterous-Hand Morphology Design
all_scored.summary: Dexterous hand design demands repeated expert work across geometry, robot-description code, collision debugging, grasp initialization, and policy training. We present Task2Hand, a Skill: a specification package that turns a functional manipulation brief into a parameterized hand model and routes every candidate through cost-ordered contact, dynamics, and learning gates. Each gate returns a status and an evidence record; on failure, the Skill records the earliest blocker, revises one bounded parameter group, and reruns the cheaper gates. The agent generates, validates, and trains autonomously within declared bounds, and escalates trade-offs, plateaus, and conflicting evidence to a human who sets the next design direction. An evidence-driven design trajectory for bidirectional in-hand manipulation yielded SAGE Hand (Skill-Aware Generative Embodiment): four fingers, 16 actuated DoF, an integrated guiding palm, compact roots, cylindrical tips, and a collision-cleared opposable thumb. Under a matched training protocol, SAGE Hand reaches 45.6% task success on a hexagonal prism against 37.3% for the LEAP hand, and 70.8% on a bicolor cylinder against 51.6%. Dense simulated tactile input more than halves the cylinder drop rate. In a controlled iteration study, the Skill path preserves capture at 164/165 trials while the path without the Skill degrades to 14/165, confirming that the gates act as a regression guard during refinement. Accepted candidates pack with URDF/MJCF, metrics, checkpoints, and a provenance manifest.

all_scored.title: FairITR: Fairness-Aware Learning of Multicategory Individualized Treatment Rules
all_scored.summary: Individualized treatment rules (ITRs) recommend treatment decisions based on individual characteristics and can improve treatment outcomes beyond traditional one-size-fits-all strategies. However, similar to other commonly used algorithmic decision-making methods, ITRs without considering model fairness may result in unfair decisions across groups defined by sensitive attributes, such as race or gender. Although extensive methods have been developed for ITR estimation, most focus solely on optimizing treatment outcomes, while research on fairness-aware ITRs remains limited. Moreover, the practical scenario of multicategory treatments is rarely considered in existing fair ITR studies. To address these gaps, we introduce a fairness notion for multicategory ITRs that requires treatment decisions to be independent of sensitive attributes, and then formulate the corresponding problem of estimating fair ITRs. To solve this problem, we further propose FairITR, a fairness-aware learning framework that jointly optimizes treatment outcomes and fairness. FairITR builds on angle-based classification for multicategory ITR learning and integrates adversarial learning with covariance-based regularization to mitigate unfairness in treatment decisions. A theoretical justification for the fairness properties induced by the adversarial debiasing mechanism is also provided. Extensive experiments on real-world datasets show that FairITR substantially reduces unfairness in ITRs while maintaining competitive treatment values relative to existing baselines.
